title: An Interview with Professor David B. Wilkins
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source summary contains no key points, description, or quotations from which to determine Professor David B. Wilkins’s position relative to the cluster synthesis.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Wilkins accepts the cluster’s training concern but develops its reform-oriented side: preserve cognitively valuable practices such as writing while rejecting untested assumptions that years of repetitive junior work are indispensable. He proposes defining essential lawyer skills and designing training around them, though he does not address the cluster’s revenue, leverage, pricing or buyer-side claims.
qs: There is no “perfect human” for doing this work, and you do not need to do these tasks repetitively for the first five years of your career.
Instead, we need to ask: what are the important skills these associates need, and how we can train them up?

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wilkins materially develops the cluster’s call for coordinated educational and employer adaptation. He identifies employer and end-user pressure as a necessary driver of law-school reform and argues that continued reliance on traditional education followed by workplace training is increasingly problematic, while also highlighting interdisciplinary learning as part of the response. He does not directly assess AI-driven displacement or junior headcount risk.
qs: For law schools to change, there has to be more pressure from the end users of law schools.
Because many legal organisations still think that if they hire in the old-fashioned way, from law schools that teach in the old-fashioned way, we can still train them once they enter the profession.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Wilkins accepts the core training risk: if AI supplies junior lawyers’ first drafts, it may remove writing-based practice needed to develop evaluative judgment. He also supports deliberate redesign rather than preserving repetitive apprenticeship tasks by default, advocating skills-led training that augments young lawyers while retaining independent learning.
qs: This raises the question: If ChatGPT can generate the first draft, how will people ever learn not just to write that first draft, but to evaluate writing?
Instead, we need to ask: what are the important skills these associates need, and how we can train them up?

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wilkins supports broad, practice-oriented reform by highlighting interdisciplinary, student-led innovation, while identifying faculty autonomy, tenure and weak employer pressure as barriers to formal curricular change. He also questions continued reliance on employers to supply training after entry.
qs: For law schools to change, there has to be more pressure from the end users of law schools.
Because you are taking away a professor’s ability to teach what they want, which – in a world in which professors have academic freedom and tenure – is extremely difficult to do.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s treatment of junior development as a design problem rather than a settled case for preserving repetitive work. He argues for retaining cognitively important practices such as writing, while replacing inherited assumptions about repetition and flawless human performance with deliberate, skills-based training.
qs: There is no “perfect human” for doing this work, and you do not need to do these tasks repetitively for the first five years of your career.
Instead, we need to ask: what are the important skills these associates need, and how we can train them up?

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s view that legal innovation depends on organisational capacity rather than technology alone. He emphasises sustained funding, strategic direction, skilled people and educational change, though he offers little detail on workflow redesign, connected data or measured implementation outcomes.
qs: I hope that continues to be true, because just as it took resources, funding and strategic direction to turn Singapore into a banking and arbitration hub, the same needs to be done for legal innovation.
To do this, you need people who understand legal innovation.

kp.k: Unauthorized-practice restrictions hinder legal self-help innovation
kp.d: Wilkins argues that unauthorized-practice restrictions concern legal technology developers and impede access to justice, requiring regulatory policy work. Nevertheless, he rejects the assumption that regulation determines innovation's direction, asserting that innovation originates from the bottom up and can occur within regulatory constraints.
qs: Developers are concerned about regulatory hurdles, especially how technologies that enable legal self-help impinges on the unauthorised practice of law.
This impacts access to justice, and requires jurisdictions to work on regulatory policy.
Innovation always comes from the bottom-up, as we have seen time and again how people have found ways to work within regulatory parameters.

kp.k: Student initiatives encourage interdisciplinary legal education
kp.d: Wilkins reports that Harvard law students' organizations addressing technology and innovation have pressured the institution to change. He identifies the university-wide innovation lab as an existing resource enabling law students to develop projects and business ideas with engineering and business students, rather than presenting a measured assessment of educational outcomes.
qs: At Harvard Law School, students have been starting organisations on law, technology and innovation.
These have put pressure on the law school as an institution.
Now, we have something called an “innovation lab” where students can work on projects and business ideas.
This means law students  can work with engineering students or business students.

kp.k: Curricular reform requires stronger employer pressure
kp.d: Wilkins explains that faculty autonomy permits new courses but that removing existing teaching is difficult under academic freedom and tenure. Echoing Dean Lee Pey Woan's observation that curricular change requires subtraction as well as addition, he calls for greater pressure from employers and users of legal skills. He criticizes reliance on traditional recruitment and subsequent workplace training as increasingly inadequate for students seeking new kinds of work.
qs: But as the Dean (Professor Lee Pey Woan, Dean, SMUYPHSOL) said in the opening panel, changing formal curricula means not just having to add, but to also subtract.
For law schools to change, there has to be more pressure from the end users of law schools.
Because many legal organisations still think that if they hire in the old-fashioned way, from law schools that teach in the old-fashioned way, we can still train them once they enter the profession.

kp.k: Singapore's legal hub strategy requires innovation investment
kp.d: Wilkins recommends that Singapore sustain resources, funding and strategic direction for legal innovation, drawing an analogy with its development as a banking and arbitration hub. He argues that maintaining a vibrant legal hub requires innovation expertise and systems directing investment toward experimentation by students and legal professionals.
qs: I hope that continues to be true, because just as it took resources, funding and strategic direction to turn Singapore into a banking and arbitration hub, the same needs to be done for legal innovation.
To remain as a vibrant legal hub, Singapore must be a hub for legal innovation.
They just need to be encouraged to do that kind of experimentation and know that there will be support and capital for them to do it.

kp.k: ChatGPT could substitute for substantial associate tasks
kp.d: In this August 2023 interview, Wilkins suggests that a well-posed legal question might elicit an answer comparable to a first-year lawyer's, with revolutionary time and cost differences. He cautions against directly publishing or submitting a first-year lawyer's work to court, then envisages AI performing tasks as well as or better than mid-year associates. These are qualitative assessments and predictions, not reported benchmark findings; he predicts substantial task substitution rather than replacement of everything.
qs: If you asked ChatGPT a good legal question today, it would give you an answer that might be as good as a first-year lawyer from a good law school.

While no one should publish or submit to court something that was handed in by a first-year lawyer, the difference in time and cost to get that document out between a first-yearer and ChatGPT is revolutionary.
Then imagine the various tasks it might start to do more quickly, and as good as, if not better than, a mid-year associate.
We need to realise that while ChatGPT is not going to replace everything, it is going to replace a huge number of things.

kp.k: AI augmentation creates opportunities and risks for learning
kp.d: Wilkins recommends exploring AI to augment young lawyers, reporting Dirk Hartung's use of ChatGPT to test his understanding of newly learned subjects. At the same time, he raises an unresolved formation problem: outsourcing first drafts could undermine learning to write and evaluate writing, because composing text itself changes and develops thinking.
qs: This question behooves us to think of how we can utilise this technology to augment our young lawyers.
To share an example, Dirk Hartung (Bucerius Law School) has been using ChatGPT to test his own knowledge about new things that he’s learning.
If ChatGPT can generate the first draft, how will people ever learn not just to write that first draft, but to evaluate writing?
We know that when you just read what others have written, it is not the same as writing it out yourself.

kp.k: Traditional training and human accuracy assumptions need testing
kp.d: Wilkins questions whether repetitive junior tasks are necessary to produce capable lawyers and recommends identifying essential skills and appropriate training instead. He reports Ironclad's Jason Boehmig saying contract analytical tools needed 99% accuracy for lawyer acceptance, contrasting this expectation with untested assumptions about exhausted associates' accuracy. The 99% figure is a reported adoption expectation, not a measured human performance rate or a comparative AI study.
qs: But has anyone ever tested or verified that these tasks are in fact necessary to produce good lawyers?
Jason shared how he had to improve the accuracy of contract analytical tools to 99%, because no lawyer will ever use a tool for understanding what is in a contract that is less than 99% accurate.
We just assume that it is 99% because they are humans, and because they are smart and well-trained.
There is no “perfect human” for doing this work, and you do not need to do these tasks repetitively for the first five years of your career.

kp.k: Access to justice requires affordability and public technological literacy
kp.d: Wilkins challenges claims that free ChatGPT has democratized AI, noting that the most advanced versions already cost money and predicting future versions are unlikely to be free. He argues that information technology disproportionately helps those able to interpret information, so ordinary citizens—not only lawyers—need technological understanding. His WebMD analogy illustrates technology helping people ask better questions of professionals and public authorities.
qs: Well, the most advanced versions are already not free, and it is unlikely they will be for future iterations of ChatGPT.
This applies to information technology more generally – it tends to improve access most for people who know how to use the information.
It has to be that ordinary citizens are also able to use technology to get access to justice – much like how WebMD helps me, as a layperson, ask better questions of my doctor.

kp.k: Market incentives leave underserved users needing subsidized solutions
kp.d: Wilkins argues that much technology-enabled access to justice will require government subsidy because it will not be profitable, while startups' profit incentives favor wealthy users. He identifies subsidy or alternative developer revenue models as necessary options, alongside public understanding that government provision requires taxation and private provision requires monetization.
qs: Much of this, however, will need to be subsidised by the government, because doing it is not going to be profitable.
If we leave it to legal tech start-ups, the profit incentive means they are going to develop solutions for the well-heeled.
But to help those who are not of means, one either needs to subsidise it, or figure out other ways for the developers to make money.
If governments are to provide it, people need to pay more taxes.

kp.k: Software providers could assume pro bono-like responsibilities
kp.d: Wilkins tentatively proposes free licensing of some legal technology software as an analogue to law-firm pro bono. Citing Brad Smith's comparison between contemporary technology and banking in the 1930s, he anticipates greater technology regulation and raises open questions about government enforcement, disclosure, consumer expectations and choosing providers for responsibility rather than speed alone. These are proposals and analogies, not established obligations.
qs: Maybe it is that legal tech companies might need to license some of their software for free – like how law firms do pro bono, perhaps that should be a responsibility for software companies to do the same.
Brad Smith (Microsoft) once said that technology today is where banking was in the 1930s.
How much should it be enforced by governments? How much should be about disclosure and the expectations of consumers?
How do we educate consumers to choose tech companies not just based on their speed and efficiency, but their responsibility?

kp.k: Young lawyers should demand credible organizational technology strategies
kp.d: Wilkins urges young lawyers to shape technological change actively, understand technologies' fundamentals and data practices, and question educational institutions and employers about their AI strategies. He advises seeking another job if an employer has no answer, grounding this advice in his assertion that competition for talent gives young professionals bargaining power and that organizations without future strategies may not survive.
qs: Since your world is going to be shaped by technology, you need to be an active participant in shaping it.
You need to educate yourself, not just about how to use technology, but the fundamentals of what it’s doing.
You should then ask of your educational institutions and employers you work for: what is your strategy for dealing with AI, or other emerging technologies?
And if they do not have an answer for that, look for another job.
You need to know that there is a war for talent out there, and talent always wins.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins predicts substantial substitution of legal tasks, alongside opportunities to augment lawyers, reshape training and expand public access to legal knowledge; he does not predict complete replacement of lawyers.
pts.d: Professor David B. Wilkins claims that ChatGPT can already produce an answer to a well-posed legal question that might match a first-year lawyer from a good law school, with a revolutionary difference in production time and cost. He anticipates it performing various tasks faster and as well as, or better than, mid-level associates, while expressly rejecting replacement of everything. On training, he identifies opportunities for self-testing and augmentation, but warns that delegating first drafts raises questions about how lawyers learn writing and evaluation, because writing itself develops thought. He challenges the assumption that years of repetitive junior work are necessary for competence. On access to justice, he argues that free availability alone does not democratise benefits: advanced versions cost money and information helps those able to interpret it. Public technological literacy could help citizens question lawyers and officials more effectively, but provision for disadvantaged users will require subsidies or alternative monetisation because commercial incentives favour affluent customers. More broadly, he identifies unauthorised-practice restrictions as obstacles to legal self-help technologies and argues that Singapore's continued standing as a legal hub depends on investment in legal innovation. He urges young lawyers to demand AI strategies from employers and educational institutions, warning conditionally that organisations without a future strategy may not survive.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims principally rest on Wilkins's expert assessment, illustrative anecdotes and incentive-based reasoning, rather than reported comparative measurements.
pts.d: The interview supplies no benchmark, measured time or cost saving, or controlled comparison supporting the first-year-lawyer equivalence or projected mid-level task performance. Wilkins offers these as assessments and prospective illustrations. For augmentation, he recounts Dirk Hartung's use of ChatGPT to test his understanding of new material. For training, he draws on the familiar experience that writing exposes weaknesses in an idea, and questions whether conventional repetitive work has been shown to produce good lawyers. He recounts an interview with Ironclad's Jason Boehmig about a 99% accuracy requirement for contract-analysis tools to challenge the assumed accuracy of human review; this is a reported adoption threshold, not a measured ChatGPT result or a demonstrated human-machine comparison. For educational adaptation, he points to student organisations and Harvard's university-wide innovation lab as examples of bottom-up change. His access-to-justice argument relies on paid advanced versions, commercial incentives and an analogy to WebMD helping laypeople ask better questions. These supporting anecdotes remain evidence cited by Wilkins, rather than independently established findings in this interview.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The baseline is August 2023; future capability and market changes have no fixed deadline and are qualified by review, skills, investment and funding requirements.
pts.d: Published on 20 August 2023 following the 3–4 August conference, the interview describes first-year-level answers as possible 'today', conditional on a good legal question. Wilkins's analogy explicitly cautions against publishing or submitting a first-year lawyer's work directly, qualifying the suggestion that equivalent AI output is ready for reliance without human checking. Mid-level task performance is prospective ('imagine' and 'might'), not a claim of demonstrated capability. He describes AI as becoming exponentially more powerful and approaching a tipping point, but provides no date or quantitative trajectory. Training applications are only beginning to be explored, while institutional curricular change is slow and requires stronger employer pressure. Singapore's innovation prospects depend on resources, strategic direction, capital and support for experimentation. Public benefits depend on citizens' ability to use technology and on sustainable provision for people unable to pay. Government subsidies and alternative developer revenue are proposed conditions; free software licensing is floated as a possible responsibility, not reported as an established requirement. Generational change is expected 'very quickly', without a precise horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are junior and mid-level lawyers, legal educators and employers, Singapore's innovation ecosystem, legal-technology developers, and citizens—especially those unable to afford legal help.
pts.d: First-year lawyers face automation of drafting and question-answering tasks, while mid-level associates are identified as a prospective next capability comparison; the interview does not quantify job losses, headcount reductions or staffing ratios. Young lawyers could gain learning aids but risk losing opportunities to develop writing and evaluative skills unless training is redesigned. Law schools face pressure for interdisciplinary and technology-related learning, and employers are urged to articulate an AI strategy to attract future talent. Singapore's government, legal institutions, students and innovators are positioned as participants in sustaining a competitive legal hub through investment and experimentation. Developers of self-help tools face regulatory hurdles; commercial legal-tech companies are expected to prioritise affluent customers unless incentives change. Disadvantaged citizens may gain more effective access to justice through supported, usable technology, rather than mere access to information. Governments, taxpayers and software providers are identified as potential funders or enablers of that access.
